sources.title: HFHR: Tęcza nie obraża. Wyrok uniewinniający utrzymany
sources.rights_note: Retained account from the earlier source review. This approval did not retrieve the page again. Not the appeal judgment. Not redistributed. Quotation retained: “12 stycznia 2022 r. Sąd Okręgowy w Płocku utrzymał w mocy wyrok uniewinniający trzy aktywistki oskarżone o obrazę uczuć religijnych za to, że w 2019 r. rozpowszechniały naklejki z wizerunkiem Matki Bożej Częstochowskiej z tęczową aureolą. Wyrok jest prawomocny.” Quotation retained: “Sąd drugiej instancji 12 stycznia 2022 utrzymał w mocy zaskarżony wyrok i uniewinnił aktywistki. Sąd Okręgowy w Płocku zaznaczył w uzasadnieniu, że wniesione apelacje były bezzasadne.” Quotation retained: “Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka złożyła w sprawie opinię przyjaciela sądu.” English translation: On 12 January 2022 the Regional Court in Płock upheld the acquitting judgment of three activists accused of offending religious feelings for distributing, in 2019, stickers with the image of Our Lady of Częstochowa with a rainbow halo. The judgment is final. The second-instance court said the appeals were unfounded. HFHR said it filed an amicus opinion. The page date is 13 January 2022. The event date is stored separately as 12 January 2022.

sources.title: KPH: Tęcza nie obraża – końcowy wyrok Sądu Najwyższego
sources.rights_note: Page dated 28 marca 2024. Read 10 October 2026. KPH says it takes part as a social party, represented by adw. Marcin Pawelec-Jakowiecki. Not the Supreme Court order. Not redistributed. Quotation: “Dzisiaj (28 marca) w Sądzie Najwyższym odbyła się rozprawa kasacyjna ws. trzech aktywistek oskarżonych o obrazę uczuć religijnych poprzez rozwieszanie naklejek z wizerunkiem matki boskiej częstochowskiej z tęczową aureolą. Sąd oddalił kasacje złożone przez pełnomocników ubocznych oskarżycieli posiłkowych, a kasacja Prokuratora Rejonowego w Płocku została skutecznie cofnięta. Sąd Najwyższy uznał, iż kasacje wniesione przez pełnomocników Kai Godek i Tadeusza Łebkowskiego są bezzasadne w stopniu oczywistym (postanowienie Sądu Najwyższego z dnia 28 marca 2024 r., sygn. akt V KK 430/22).” Quotation: “Elżbieta Podleśna, Joanna Gzyra-Iskandar i Anna Prus rozwiesiły w okolicy kościoła naklejki z wizerunkiem matki boskiej częstochowskiej z tęczową aureolą.” Quotation: “Sądy dwóch instancji (wyrok Sądu Rejonowego w Płocku z 2.03.2021 r. oraz Sądu Okręgowego w Płocku z 12.01.2022 r.) uniewinniły aktywistki w całości od zarzucanego im czynu.” Quotation: “W dzisiejszym wyroku Sąd Najwyższy oddalił kasacje pełnomocników ubocznych oskarżycieli posiłkowych (Kai Godek i Tadeusza Łebkowskiego), złożone od wyroku sądu II instancji.” English translation: Today (28 March) a cassation hearing was held in the Supreme Court in the case of three activists accused of offending religious feelings by putting up stickers of Our Lady of Częstochowa with a rainbow halo. The court dismissed the cassations filed by counsel for the auxiliary prosecutors, and the cassation of the District Prosecutor in Płock was effectively withdrawn. The Supreme Court found that the cassations brought by counsel for Kaja Godek and Tadeusz Łebkowski were obviously groundless (Supreme Court order of 28 March 2024, case V KK 430/22). Elżbieta Podleśna, Joanna Gzyra-Iskandar, and Anna Prus put up the stickers near the church. Courts of two instances, the District Court in Płock on 2 March 2021 and the Regional Court in Płock on 12 January 2022, acquitted them in full. A later sentence on the same page calls that dismissal today's judgment. The page uses both postanowienie and wyrok. The form of the decision is not resolved. The withdrawal and the dismissal are different actions.

sources.title: Rzeczpospolita: Jest decyzja SN. Bez kary za Matkę Boską z tęczową aureolą
sources.rights_note: Different article from the 13 January 2022 rp.pl piece that draws on HFHR. Publication line 28.03.2024 14:43. Does not cite KPH. Not the Supreme Court order. Not redistributed. Quotation: “To konsekwencja decyzji Sądu Najwyższego, który oddalił w czwartek jako oczywiście bezzasadne kasacje w tej sprawie Kai Godek i płockiego księdza.” Quotation: “Zareagowały na to trzy aktywistki: Elżbieta Podleśna, Joanna Gzyra-Iskandar i Anna Prus.” Quotation: “W marcu 2021 r. Sąd Rejonowy w Płocku uniewinnił kobiety.” Quotation: “Wyrok uniewinniający utrzymał w styczniu 2022 r. płocki sąd okręgowy.” Quotation: “W ostatnich dniach płocka prokuratura wycofała jednak swoją kasację.” Quotation: “Sąd Najwyższy ostatecznie oddalił w czwartek pozostałe kasacje jako oczywiście bezzasadne.” Quotation: “Sygnatura akt: V KK 430/22.” English translation: This follows the Supreme Court's decision, which on Thursday dismissed as obviously groundless the cassations in this case of Kaja Godek and the Płock priest. Three activists reacted: Elżbieta Podleśna, Joanna Gzyra-Iskandar, and Anna Prus. In March 2021 the District Court in Płock acquitted the women. The acquitting judgment was upheld in January 2022 by the Płock regional court. In recent days the Płock prosecution withdrew its cassation. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the remaining cassations on Thursday as obviously groundless. Case signature V KK 430/22. The phrase in recent days is not a date. The publication timestamp is not the withdrawal date. This article names the Płock priest and does not spell Tadeusz Łebkowski.

arguments.institutional_affiliation: City University of New York; TrialWatch Expert Panel. ABA Center for Human Rights staff helped draft the report.
arguments.disclaimer_text: The views expressed herein represent the opinions of the authors. They have not been reviewed or approved by the House of Delegates or the Board of Governors of the American Bar Association and, accordingly, should not be construed as representing the position of the Association or any of its entities. Furthermore, nothing in this report should be considered legal advice for specific cases. Additionally, the views expressed in this report are not necessarily those of the Clooney Foundation for Justice.
arguments.summary: The report argues that Article 196 is not precise and is so broad that it gives the authorities unfettered discretion.
arguments.reasons: The executive summary says the offense turns on offending religious feelings, which it calls a subjective concept.
arguments.principle: A restriction on expression must be precise, clear, and accessible.
arguments.application: Article 196 criminalizes offending religious feelings by public insult, and the report says that standard gives charging discretion.
arguments.remedy_requested: Not in the argument passage. Printed p. 4, PDF page 5: “The prosecution’s appeal in the present case, which is scheduled to be heard on November 10, should likewise be rejected.” and “While the legislature should repeal Article 196…” Printed p. 31, PDF page 32, conclusion: “on November 10 the appellate court in Plock should dismiss the prosecution’s appeal against the acquittal.” Same page, Recommendations from Professor Lisa Davis: to the Polish legislature, Article 196 should be repealed; to the Polish judiciary, the court should dismiss the prosecution’s appeal against the acquittal of Podlesna, Prus, and Gzyra-Iskandar. The November 10 sentence does not restate the year.
arguments.passage: Article 196 is not precise, clear, or accessible. In criminalizing acts that “offend the religious feelings of other persons” through public insult, by nature a subjective concept, Article 196 is so broad as to afford the authorities unfettered discretion in its application, making it ripe for abuse.
arguments.location_ref: Fairness report, printed p. 3, PDF page 4
arguments.legal_authorities: Article 196 of the Polish Criminal Code; ICCPR; ECHR, as cited in the report.
arguments.public_limitation: This is what the named author wrote. It is not a court finding. No reviewed record establishes how a court received the argument. That absence is not a finding that the court ignored it. II K 296/20 identifies the original trial cited in the report, not an appeal docket. The PDF cover says November 2021. The CFJ report page says Published 21 January 2022.

arguments.summary: The report argues that the prosecution failed necessity and proportionality because the posters were not an exceptionally grave speech offense.
arguments.reasons: The executive summary reserves criminal speech prosecutions for exceptionally grave acts such as incitement to genocide and terrorism, and says the posters did not reach that gravity.
arguments.principle: Criminal prosecutions for speech offenses should be reserved for exceptionally grave acts.
arguments.application: Posting stickers and posters of a rainbow halo did not, in the report's account, reach that level of gravity.
arguments.remedy_requested: Not in the argument passage. Printed p. 4, PDF page 5: “The prosecution’s appeal in the present case, which is scheduled to be heard on November 10, should likewise be rejected.” and “While the legislature should repeal Article 196…” Printed p. 31, PDF page 32, conclusion: “on November 10 the appellate court in Plock should dismiss the prosecution’s appeal against the acquittal.” Same page, Recommendations from Professor Lisa Davis: to the Polish legislature, Article 196 should be repealed; to the Polish judiciary, the court should dismiss the prosecution’s appeal against the acquittal of Podlesna, Prus, and Gzyra-Iskandar. The November 10 sentence does not restate the year.
arguments.passage: Third, the case against the accused failed to meet necessity and proportionality requirements. With respect to this requirement, international and regional bodies have made clear that criminal prosecutions for speech offenses should be reserved for exceptionally grave acts, such as incitement to genocide and terrorism. The accused’s posting of stickers and posters featuring a rainbow halo clearly did not rise to this level of gravity.
arguments.location_ref: Fairness report, printed p. 4, PDF page 5
arguments.legal_authorities: ICCPR and ECHR standards, as cited in the report.
arguments.public_limitation: This is what the named author wrote. It is not a court finding. No reviewed record establishes how a court received the argument. That absence is not a finding that the court ignored it. II K 296/20 identifies the original trial cited in the report, not an appeal docket. The PDF cover says November 2021. The CFJ report page says Published 21 January 2022.

arguments.disclaimer_text: The legal assessment and conclusions expressed in this report are those of the author and not necessarily those of the Clooney Foundation for Justice or any of the author's affiliated organizations.
arguments.summary: The report argues that Tam Tak-chi was convicted under a vague and overbroad sedition statute for political statements.
arguments.reasons: The executive summary describes the colonial-era ordinance as overbroad and as criminalizing political speech.
arguments.principle: A criminal statute used against speech must not be vague or overbroad.
arguments.application: The report applies that criticism to the sedition charges for political statements, including slogans and criticism of the National Security Law and the police.
arguments.remedy_requested: Not stated in this passage. The conclusion on printed p. 51, PDF page 52, grades the trial D and says the conviction and sentence infringed expression and assembly rights. It does not state a requested court order. That is a limit of the pages read, not a finding that no other page requests a remedy.
arguments.passage: In the proceedings against him, Tam Tak-chi was denied his procedural rights to a fair trial—in particular, the right to an impartial tribunal—and was charged and convicted under a vague and overbroad statute for making political statements.
arguments.location_ref: Fairness report, printed p. 3, PDF page 4
arguments.legal_authorities: Crimes Ordinance sedition provisions, as discussed in the report.
arguments.public_limitation: This is the author's criticism of the conviction under the sedition statute. The conviction predates the report. No passage was identified in the later appeal judgments that shows the court responding to this report. That is not a finding that the court ignored the argument. The appeal copies have not been authenticated against an official host.

arguments.disclaimer_text: The legal assessment and conclusions expressed in this report are those of the author and not necessarily those of the Clooney Foundation for Justice or any of the author's affiliated organizations.
arguments.summary: The report argues that the sentence of three years and four months plus a fine is a disproportionate sanction for political speech and organising an unauthorised assembly.
arguments.reasons: The executive summary states the sanction after describing the conviction and the 20 April 2022 sentence. The report is later than that sentence.
arguments.principle: Sanctions on expression and assembly must be proportionate.
arguments.application: A sentence of three years and four months, plus a fine, for political speech and organising an unauthorised assembly. The quotation does not divide that punishment between expression and assembly.
arguments.remedy_requested: Not stated in this passage. The conclusion on printed p. 51, PDF page 52, says the conviction and sentence infringed expression and assembly rights and assigns a grade of D. It does not state a requested court order. That is a limit of the pages read.
arguments.passage: Further, the sentence in this case—three years and four months in prison in addition to a fine—for political speech and organising an unauthorised assembly—are disproportionate sanctions on the exercise of the rights to freedom of expression and assembly.
arguments.location_ref: Fairness report, printed p. 2, PDF page 3
arguments.legal_authorities: Rights to freedom of expression and assembly, as invoked in the report.
arguments.public_limitation: The quoted punishment covers political speech and organising an unauthorised assembly together. It does not say that every part of the sentence was solely for expression, and this record does not allocate the sentence by count. A later passage in the report, and an official press summary, itemize counts. That itemization is not this claim. The sentence predates the report, so the report is not a response to a later court.

arguments.institutional_affiliation: Counsel for Tam Tak-chi in the Court of Appeal
arguments.summary: Counsel argued that section 9 imposes a disproportionate restriction on freedom of expression because the prosecution does not need to prove an incitement to violence.
arguments.reasons: Paragraph 139 summarizes this proportionality submission. Paragraphs 132 to 144 are the proportionality discussion. This is counsel's argument, not the May 2022 report.
arguments.principle: A restriction on expression must be proportionate.
arguments.application: Section 9, on counsel's submission, is a disproportionate restriction because the prosecution need not prove an incitement to violence.
arguments.remedy_requested: Leave to appeal, cited separately at paragraph 3, not in paragraph 139: leave against conviction of the sedition charges only, and against the sentences for both the sedition charges and the public-order charges.
arguments.passage: Mr Dykes argued that section 9 imposes a disproportionate restriction on the right to freedom of expression because the prosecution does not need to prove an incitement to violence.
arguments.legal_authorities: Crimes Ordinance ss. 9 and 10; Bill of Rights.
arguments.public_limitation: This is counsel's proportionality limb only, as the judgment summarizes it at paragraph 139. Paragraph 145 holds that sections 9 and 10 satisfy the proportionality test. It does not establish rejection of the legal-certainty argument, which the same judgment addresses at paragraph 131, or the slogan argument from paragraph 146. Philip Dykes SC is counsel in the appeal, not the author of the May 2022 fairness report. The text was read from a Columbia-hosted copy. A check of the official legal reference site on 9 October 2026 did not retrieve CACC 62/2022, so authenticity is not established.

outcomes.description: Sentence imposed on 20 April 2022. The official press summary of [2022] HKDC 343 states that it is not part of the judgment and that the total sentence is 40 months together with a HK$5,000 fine. The May 2022 fairness report states the same aggregate for political speech and organising an unauthorised assembly. This is the original sentence, not a later modification. The charge-by-charge breakdown in the press summary is not stored as the report's claim.
outcomes.finality: appeal later dismissed, on the texts read
outcomes.public_limitation: This is the sentence imposed on 20 April 2022, not a later modification. An official District Court press summary of [2022] HKDC 343 states that the summary is not part of the judgment and confirms an aggregate of 40 months and a HK$5,000 fine. That summary itemizes counts. This record does not use the itemization as the fairness report's claim, which covers speech and unauthorized assembly together. The Court of Appeal text that recites the sentence was read from a Columbia-hosted copy whose authenticity against an official host is not established.

outcomes.description: Later development in the same proceeding. The Court of Appeal judgment of 7 March 2024, read from a Columbia-hosted copy, says: “We accordingly refuse to grant leave to appeal against conviction and dismiss the appeal.” Paragraph 177 likewise refuses leave to appeal against sentence and dismisses that appeal. A text search of the copy found no Wilmshurst, TrialWatch, or Clooney. The dismissal is the outcome. It is not a documented response to the May 2022 report.
outcomes.finality: further appeal to the Court of Final Appeal followed

It does not establish that the court responded to the May 2022 fairness report.

receptions.passage: In conclusion, we hold that sections 9 and 10 of the CO and accordingly the Sedition Charges satisfy the proportionality test.
receptions.location_ref: CACC 62/2022, [2024] HKCA 231, paragraphs 132–145; holding at paragraph 145
receptions.observer_note: Private comparison, 9 October 2026. Paragraphs 90–102 reject reading in an intention to incite violence and leave constitutionality open. Paragraph 131 rejects counsel's legal-certainty submissions. Paragraphs 132–145 are the proportionality limb; paragraph 139 is counsel's incitement point; paragraph 145 is only the proportionality holding. Paragraph 146 onward is a separate slogan argument. Do not treat paragraph 145 as disposing of legal certainty or the slogan. Counsel is not Wilmshurst. reasoning_checked stays false.
receptions.public_limitation: This is counsel's proportionality limb only, as the judgment summarizes it at paragraph 139. Paragraph 145 holds that sections 9 and 10 satisfy the proportionality test. It does not establish rejection of the legal-certainty argument, which the same judgment addresses at paragraph 131, or the slogan argument from paragraph 146. Philip Dykes SC is counsel in the appeal, not the author of the May 2022 fairness report. The text was read from a Columbia-hosted copy. A check of the official legal reference site on 9 October 2026 did not retrieve CACC 62/2022, so authenticity is not established.
